Let me check the latest (post-Sept 23 status report).I couldn't open the Metaculus page (question 45810, opened Sept 28, 2026), so I can't tell you what it says right now. What follows comes from news coverage.

**Bottom line:** Based on current information, this resolves **No**. No part of the building has been demolished. A court order requires 30 days' written notice before any demolition, so the earliest a lawful demolition could start is about late October to November, and only if notice were filed right away.

**Timeline**
- **Early Feb 2026:** Trump announced the center would close on July 4 for about two years of renovation. He called it "Construction, Revitalization, and Complete Rebuilding," but the extent of the "complete rebuilding" was unclear.
- **May–June:** Judge Christopher Cooper ruled that the center illegally added Trump's name to the building and ordered it removed. The center complied in June but left a tarp and scaffolding where the name had been. Cooper also blocked the closure plans.
- **Aug 25:** For the first time, DOJ lawyers raised demolition in a court filing. They said that without the renovation, the center "will deteriorate further into an unsafe, decrepit structure that will be required to be taken down" and floated an outdoor amphitheater for the site.
- **Mid-Sept:** The board, chaired by Trump, voted to go ahead with the $257 million renovation project. Cooper rejected another attempt to put Trump's name on the building. The administration appealed, and Trump posted that the center "is destined to doom" without the repairs.
- **Sept 16:** The main building closed "temporarily," with fencing put up around it. Trump said the center could be "ripped down" and was photographed looking at a poster reading "Kennedy Center DEMOLISHED." A center spokesperson said "nothing is being demolished". A witness said in a filing that a "forklift run into and hit the pillars".
- **Sept 17:** Cooper ordered the 30 days' written notice before any changes, "including but not limited to any 'demolition'". Emergency repairs can continue.
- **~Sept 23–24:** The DOJ filed the required status report. It lists hazards such as collapsing ceiling panels and water getting into transformers, but "contains no finding that the center needs to be demolished". The executive director said the center could reopen once the safety issues are addressed.
- **Sept 22 (Trump post, per The Hill):** Trump said the renovations won't begin unless the court approves the board's plan to put his name on the building. That suggests he's using demolition as a bargaining threat, not an active plan.

**What to watch before Jan 1, 2027**
- Any 30-day demolition notice filed with Cooper's court.
- Weekly decisions on whether to extend the temporary closure.
- The administration's appeal of the naming ruling.
- Discovery in Rep. Beatty's lawsuit, which Cooper has allowed to cover the demolition question.
- Whether the Aug–Sept threat was bluster.

**Base rates and context**
- **Against:** Tearing down a congressionally designated memorial while a court injunction is in place would be close to unprecedented.
- **For:** Trump quickly demolished the East Wing of the White House in 2025 despite objections.
- **Resolution risk:** The criteria use a "de minimis" threshold, so partial interior demolition done as part of the renovation could count. That makes resolution less clear-cut than a full teardown would.

I didn't find any prediction-market prices.

letra_pequena:
The center will be deemed substantially demolished if more than a *de minimis* portion of the structure is intentionally destroyed.

***
This question's information (resolution criteria, fine print, background info, etc) is synced with an [original identical question](https://www.metaculus.com/questions/45810) which opened on 2026-09-28 17:00:00. This question will resolve based on the resolution criteria and fine print of the linked original question. However, if this question would resolve differently than the original question, then this question will be annulled. razonamientos:
(a) **Time left:** About three months, until January 1, 2027.  
(b) **Status quo:** No demolition has occurred; if nothing changes, the answer is No.  
(c) **Reference class:** Demolition of a major, federally designated memorial within three months, amid active litigation, is exceptionally rare. I would put the ordinary short-term base rate well below 5%; Trump’s explicit threat and control of the board raise this case above that baseline.  
(d) **No scenario:** The closure and safety repairs continue, but the administration neither announces nor carries out substantial demolition before the deadline.  
(e) **Yes scenario:** Trump orders demolition despite the legal obstacles, or renovation work intentionally destroys a meaningful portion of the structure.  
(f) **Resolution technicality:** A complete teardown is unnecessary. Intentional destruction of **more than a *de minimis* portion** counts, including potentially work described as renovation.

The demolition threat is credible enough to take seriously, particularly given the East Wing precedent. But the reported status filing identifies safety hazards rather than a need to demolish, a center spokesperson has denied demolition plans, and the court’s notice requirement creates time for scrutiny. With no reported demolition notice or concrete plan and only three months remaining, No remains substantially more likely.

Probability: 15%

(a) **Time left:** About 3 months, until January 1, 2027. Any demolition would be public and visible right away.

(b) **Status quo:** The building stands. It is closed and fenced "temporarily" for safety repairs. A court order requires 30 days' written notice before any changes, and no demolition notice has been filed. The status quo outcome is No.

(c) **Reference class:** Demolishing a major federally protected or memorial building within about 3 months, while a court injunction and active litigation are in place. The base rate is very low, under 5%. The main counterexample is the East Wing demolition in 2025. That was done quickly, but it involved executive-controlled White House property and no injunction was in effect.

(d) **No scenario:** Trump keeps using demolition as leverage over the naming dispute. On September 22 he said renovations won't start unless his name goes on the building. Emergency safety repairs continue, and the appeal on the naming ruling drags on past January. Nothing is filed under the notice requirement, or a notice is filed but then challenged and enjoined. The building remains intact through year-end.

(e) **Yes scenario:** The administration files a 30-day notice in October, citing structural hazards. Cooper fails to block it, or the D.C. Circuit or Supreme Court stays his order. Crews begin tearing down parts of the structure in November or December, possibly framed as "renovation" gutting of the interior. Alternatively, the administration defies the order outright, as it moved fast on the East Wing.

(f) **Technicalities in the resolution criteria:**
- "More than a *de minimis* portion of the structure intentionally destroyed" means partial demolition as part of a renovation could count, not only a full teardown.
- Emergency repairs, such as removing collapsing ceiling panels, are probably de minimis or not "destruction."
- The renovation has not started, and Trump has conditioned it on the naming approval.
- The 30-day notice pushes any lawful action to late October at the earliest. After that, likely further litigation would follow.

On balance, the demolition talk looks mostly like bargaining. There is still a small tail risk from Trump's willingness to act abruptly and from the loose de minimis threshold.

Probability: 6%

(a) **Time left:** About 93 days, through December 31, 2026.

(b) **Status quo:** No demolition has been reported. The center is closed, and a court order requires 30 days’ written notice before physical changes, including demolition.

(c) **Reference class:** Substantial demolition of a prominent, legally protected public building during active litigation is rare on a three-month horizon. I would put the ordinary baseline in the low single digits, though this case is unusually volatile.

(d) **No scenario:** The threatened demolition remains leverage in the dispute over the center’s name and renovations; safety repairs proceed without destroying a meaningful part of the structure.

(e) **Yes scenario:** The administration gives notice and proceeds after a court ruling—or acts despite the order—and intentionally removes a meaningful portion of the building before year-end.

(f) **Resolution technicality:** A full teardown is **not** required. More than a *de minimis* portion intentionally destroyed could count, including demolition undertaken as part of renovations.

The explicit threat and the low threshold raise the risk above the baseline. Still, the short deadline, court scrutiny, and the center spokesperson’s denial of demolition make **No** considerably more likely.

Probability: 12%
